guards.rule: A room's listed functional pieces (stove, fridge, cabinets) must be built and visible; if the render shows an empty shell, the build stage failed to place them.
A living room of this size must have a sofa and a coffee table as its anchor group; if missing, the agent must place the standard living group.
A camera for a room must frame the room's main functional group, not a blank wall or partition.

Under a sloped ceiling, the furniture agent must select a bed model with a maximum height that fits the clearance; if no library model fits, the build stage must generate a parametric bed that respects the ceiling height.
A camera for a room must frame the room's main functional group, not a door or wall corner.
A camera for a room must frame the room's main functional group, not a wall or cabinet face.
Exterior site items (trees, ground) must use high-quality, photorealistic assets, not low-poly placeholders.
Scene checks must pass; if a check fails, the build stage must be re-run to fix the geometry.
The exterior ground must be textured and realistic, not a flat, untextured plane.
Pieces placed by the decor stage must be preserved by the agent stage; if a piece is missing, the agent must re-place it.
A drawn cluster larger than 4.5 m on a side in a room must be split into individual pieces or marked as a single built-in element, not left untyped.
Outdoor site areas like balconies and verandas must have their edges and steps built as part of the site model, even if the main outline is not built.
A hall/entry camera must frame the room's defining piece (shoe cabinet, stair) and its function, not a bare corner.
A bathroom's wet fixtures (bathtub, washbasin, toilet) must not overlap; the fitter must find a non-clashing position before the run is accepted.
No furniture may block the sightline or egress through a window opening.
A labelled balcony/veranda must be built with its slab, railing, supports, and the door that accesses it; a floating slab with no access is a loss.
A door on a balcony or veranda must be anchored in its frame and reach the floor of the space it opens to; a floating or mis-anchored door is a build error.
A main entrance must have a legible door leaf, handle, and a clear approach (step, ramp, or canopy) so a client can identify and reach it.
A dressing room (soyunma odası) adjacent to a bedroom must be typed as a bedroom/dressing room, not 'other', so its furniture set (wardrobe + mirror + seating) is validated and completed.
A labelled veranda is a client-visible outdoor space; its absence from the model is a loss, not a good reason.
A labelled balcony is a client-visible outdoor space; its absence from the model is a loss.
A living room must hold a coherent furniture set (seating + table + anchor); a bare room with only a sofa and lamp is not acceptable.
The big loop must run enough cycles to raise the house score; stopping with 0 cycles and 147 open major points is a process failure.
A bedroom camera must frame the bed and the room's primary function; a view marked for review indicates the framing is inadequate.

When a section prints the ground floor at a non-zero datum (e.g. +0.50), the reading stage must detect the offset and re-anchor all relative level marks to the true ground floor (z=0) before any downstream stage uses them.
When a document label names a piece type at a position where no piece stands, the fit stage must place that piece type in the room at the nearest valid spot, rather than leaving the label unverified.
Furniture pieces must not overlap; the fit stage must resolve clashes by moving one piece to a valid spot within the room.
Furniture must not block windows or doors; the fit stage must move pieces clear of openings.
The set_camera tool must accept 'room' as a valid kind for interior views, or the agent must use 'interior' with correct position and target parameters to frame the room.

When a bed's headboard is slightly off the wall (e.g., 0.06 m), the move_piece tool should allow a small snap correction to the wall if no other valid spot exists, or the fit stage should place the bed flush with the wall initially.

When a wardrobe blocks a window, the move_piece tool should allow moving it to a different wall span if the current wall has no free space, or the fit stage should avoid placing wardrobes in front of windows.
The place_group tool should have a valid 'dressing' group definition that can fit in a 5.9 m2 room, or the fit stage should place a wardrobe and mirror in the dressing room.

When a wardrobe's front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway, the move_piece tool should allow moving it to a different wall span if the current wall has no free space, or the fit stage should ensure walkways are clear.

When a drawn piece is untyped and the AI suggests a type (e.g., desk, dresser), the retype_piece tool should allow the type if it fits the size and room, or the fit stage should type the piece correctly.

When a bed has only one nightstand but the schedule lists two, the move_piece tool should allow placing the second nightstand on the other side of the bed if space allows, or the fit stage should place both nightstands.
The swap_model tool should have a catalogue model for a pale wood coffee table, or the fit stage should choose a model that matches the room's palette.
The render stage must ensure that all rooms are furnished and lit before rendering, or the agent must place furniture and set a camera for empty rooms.
The scene stage must use high-quality tree models that match the realism of the render, or the agent must replace low-poly tree models with better ones.

The site stage must replace the default low-poly placeholder landscape with a photorealistic environment (HDRI or high-poly vegetation) that matches the project's render quality target; a flat cartoon backdrop is never acceptable for a client-ready render.

A room's primary camera must frame the room's main functional group (seating, dining, bed) and not a bare wall or a single stray piece; if the group is out of frame, re-aim the camera before judging the room's furnishing.
Two pieces of the same type placed as a pair in one room must be the same model and finish; the fit stage must not leave two different armchair models side by side.
A bathroom camera must frame the room's fixtures, not a blank wall or a window whose outdoor scene is a placeholder; if the only window shows a placeholder, aim the camera away from it.
The site stage must build a real exterior (trees, ground, sky) from the project's exterior library; a low-poly placeholder landscape is never acceptable in a client render.

A bathroom's washbasin must be placed inside the room (not in a door swing) and the room must carry its standard decor set (mirror, towel, soap, hardware); the fit stage must not leave a bathroom as a bare grey-box.
A bedroom camera must frame the bed group and main furniture, not a window whose outdoor scene is a placeholder; if the only window shows a placeholder, aim the camera away from it.
Two beds of the same type in one room must be the same model and scale; the fit stage must not leave two different bed models in one room, and a bed must not block a door.

A dresser must be a real product model with visible drawer lines, texture and a top surface; the fit stage must not leave a plain box with floating dots for handles, and the model must fit under any sloped ceiling.

A children's bedroom's bed and dresser must be real product models that match each other and the floor finish; the fit stage must not leave placeholder geometry (low-poly blob bed, plain box dresser) in a client render.

A nightstand must be a real product model that matches the room's floor and furniture finish, and it must be placed against a wall (not floating 0.34 m off); the fit stage must not leave a plain box with a clashing wood tone.

A shower/bathroom camera must frame the room's fixtures (shower, basin, toilet), not a blank corner or a window whose outdoor scene is a placeholder; if the only window shows a placeholder, aim the camera away from it.
A shower/bathroom camera must frame the room's fixtures (shower, basin, toilet), not a blank corner; the camera must not be jammed against the shower glass and a tiled wall.

An interior camera must be placed at a standing eye height (1.5 m) in the middle of the room, looking at the room's center, with a wide lens (24-28 mm) to show the whole space; it must never be pressed against a wall or piece.

Every window in the building must be visible in at least one render (either an interior view looking out, or an exterior view showing the facade); if a window is not visible in any current camera, a new camera must be added or an existing one adjusted to include it.

Exterior renders must use a realistic ground model (planar or tin) and site items (trees, shrubs) that match the project's style; crude 'lollipop' trees and flat untextured ground are not acceptable for client presentation.

Doors are not furniture pieces and cannot be swapped using swap_model; their appearance is controlled by the door model library or material slots. If a door looks generic, the door model must be selected from the library during the building stage, or the material slot for doors must be set to a realistic finish.
Window and door frames must have a material that contrasts with the facade and matches the project's style; generic flat grey frames are not acceptable for a stylish home.
Exterior renders must use a realistic ground model (planar or tin); a flat untextured green plane is not acceptable for client presentation.

Kitchen counters must have a realistic countertop material (e.g., quartz, granite) and handles; a plain untextured white box is not acceptable for client presentation.
Furniture should be placed to create balanced compositions; a sideboard pushed into a corner with a large empty wall beside it is not acceptable.
Armchairs should be part of a seating arrangement, not pushed flat against a wall under a window; they should be angled towards the center of the room or the coffee table.
A wet-room fixture that reads as floating or cut off at a wall edge must be re-placed against its host wall or counter in the next agent round when its model is pinned and cannot be swapped.
A decorative accent that clashes with the room's stated palette and whose model is pinned must be replaced in the next agent round with a model that passes the room's height and fit caps.
The exterior ground plane must carry a textured material (grass, soil, or paver) rather than a flat untextured colour, so it does not read as a default viewport floor.
The DWG reading stage must parse ATTDEF entities and expose their attribute values to the ledger, so that labelled spaces, areas, and annotations carried in block attributes are not silently dropped.

When site decor symbols are read on multiple levels, the site stage must deduplicate them (keeping the ground-floor set) and flag any that are not used, rather than leaving 42 untyped symbols unplaced.
When a room outline holds two labels (e.g. 'Salon' and 'YEMEK BÖLÜMÜ'), the reading stage must split the outline into two rooms so each labelled space is its own room in the model.
The reading stage must associate printed area labels with their corresponding room outlines so that area checks can be run against the model.

When walls are drawn as face lines on multiple layers, the reading stage must include all wall primitives that close the labelled rooms, not just those on the single chosen layer, to avoid missing wall segments.
When the plan draws an object in a room that is not built in the model, the furniture stage must identify the object's type and place it in the next agent round.
When a decor item's host piece is not built, the decor must be deferred to the next agent round, after the host is re-placed.
When a piece's type is not allowed in its room (e.g. a sofa in a bedroom), the reading stage must flag it for re-typing or removal, rather than keeping it unverified.

When a room outline holds the labels of two rooms, the reading must split the outline at the wall between the two labelled zones (or flag the missing wall) instead of keeping one label and dropping the other; a dining zone labelled inside a living room is a separate room or a sub-zone, not a lost label.

When an elevation's openings cannot be checked against the plans because the north arrow is missing, the reading must infer the orientation from the plan's north arrow or the site context, and flag the elevation as 'orientation unverified' rather than skipping the check entirely.

A drawn section whose ends do not align with the roof outline (offset > 0.30 m) or whose roof line is non-monotonic must be flagged as a non-corresponding section and excluded from point-by-point roof checks, rather than failing the check silently.

guards.rule: Elevations without a view bearing or side must be assigned a default orientation based on their position relative to the plan, or flagged as uncheckable with a clear reason, rather than silently failing the comparison.

When a nightstand cannot be snapped to a wall due to doors/windows blocking all free places within 1.2 m, the fitting stage should allow a small offset (up to 0.10 m) from the wall or place it freestanding next to the bed, rather than refusing all moves.
The agent must only use material look IDs that exist in the project's vocabulary; the vocabulary should be exposed to the agent in its context so it does not guess look names.
Kitchen fittings (sink, wall cabinets) should be built at the library level (with proper textures and details) rather than falling back to parametric meshes when no library model is available.
Toilet models in the library should include seat covers and basic decor (e.g., spare toilet paper) to avoid a sterile, incomplete appearance in renders.
Bathroom fixtures and tiles should be selected from a higher-quality library set to avoid a cheap, institutional look in renders.
Bed models in the library should include more substantial headboards and frames to avoid a plain, low-profile appearance in client-ready renders.
Nightstand models in the library should be more stylish and cohesive with the room's furniture set to avoid a generic, unstyled appearance.
Door models in the library should include more detailed handles and finishes to avoid a cheap, generic appearance in stylish projects.

A stair or landing that is the only vertical circulation of a level must be built with a full parametric stair model (treads, risers, stringers and a proper balustrade), never as a bare platform with a glass guard; a platform-only representation is a defect, not a style choice.

Interior doors must be built with a styled door model (panelled or flush with a proper frame and handle) matching the project's finish, never as a plain flat slab; a generic slab door is a defect in a client presentation.
A floor lamp must be built with a proper library model (a real lamp with a shade and stem), never as a low-poly box placeholder; a placeholder lamp is a defect.

Exterior wall surfaces and plinths must be built with textured materials (stone, render, brick) matching the project's finish, never as untextured flat surfaces; bare material is a defect in a client presentation.
A stone path or paving leading to an entrance must be built with a textured paving model, never as a rough untextured mesh with visible cracks; a placeholder path is a defect.
Untyped drawn pieces must be typed by the reading stage before the build stage; the build stage must not silently drop untyped pieces without a record.

A labelled outdoor area (veranda, balcony, terrace) in the documents must be built as a site platform with its drawn outline, even when the outline is open or partially defined; 'no outline' is not a valid reason to drop a labelled site area.

A labelled veranda, balcony or terrace in the documents must be built as a site area (floor slab, railing, and a door from the adjacent room) even when its outline is incomplete; an unbuildable outline is a reason to flag the drawing, not to silently drop the element.

A room typed 'other' that the documents name as a dressing room (soyunma odası) must be furnished as a dressing room (mirror, bench or stool, wardrobe); the 'other' type must not suppress the completeness check for that room.
A room typed 'living' must be furnished as a living room (seating plus a table and a focal point such as a TV or media unit); a sofa alone does not satisfy the type.
Furniture must match the level it is placed on: a shoe cabinet belongs at the ground-floor entrance, not in an upper-floor hall, which should instead carry a console, coat hook or bench.

When two openings on the same wall are separated by less than 1.20 m, the layout engine must verify that the intervening wall span can accommodate a 0.60 m clear walkway; if not, it must propose moving one of the openings or adjusting the room layout to create the required clearance.

When a bed's headboard is not flush against a wall (offset > 0.02 m), the layout engine must snap it to the nearest wall if the move is within 0.30 m, or flag it for manual review if the move exceeds the drawn-lock tolerance.

When a piece blocks a door swing, the layout engine must move the piece to the nearest free position that does not intersect the door's swing arc, prioritizing positions along the wall opposite the door.

When a piece blocks a window, the layout engine must move the piece to the nearest free position that does not obstruct the window's view or access, prioritizing positions along the wall opposite the window.

When a door and a window on the same wall are separated by less than 1.20 m, the layout engine must verify that the intervening wall span can accommodate a 0.60 m clear walkway; if not, it must propose moving one of the openings or adjusting the room layout to create the required clearance.
When a desk is rendered as a floating slab, the render engine must verify that the model includes legs or support structure; if not, it must swap to a model that includes them.

When a room's main functional pieces are not visible in the render, the camera must be adjusted to include them in the frame, prioritizing a wide-angle lens and a position that captures the entire worktop and appliances.
When a living room lacks a sofa or coffee table, the layout engine must add a living group (sofa, coffee table, armchairs) to anchor the space, prioritizing a sofa along the longest wall.

When a bathroom's main pieces (toilet, washbasin, bathtub) are not visible in the render, the camera must be adjusted to include them in the frame, prioritizing a wide-angle lens and a position that captures the entire room.

When a kitchen's main functional pieces (stove, fridge, wall cabinets) are not visible in the render, the camera must be adjusted to include them in the frame, prioritizing a wide-angle lens and a position that captures the entire worktop and appliances.

Every open staircase (no solid wall on one or both sides) must be built with handrails and balustrades on all open sides to meet safety standards.

For rooms with no windows or very small windows (e.g., dressing rooms, closets), the lighting system must be able to increase light by up to x10, or the camera exposure cap must be raised to +6.00 EV to allow proper exposure.

The architect's rule F2 / F3 must include a check for furniture blocking doors (F7) to ensure that no furniture blocks a door's swing or walkway, and flag any furniture that does.

The architect's rule E1 must include a check for doors that are too high to reach (X3) to ensure that all doors are at a reachable height (e.g., 0.90-2.10 m above the floor), and flag any door that is above this range.

A sofa placed under a sloped ceiling must be fitted to the ceiling clearance at its position (max height = ceiling - 0.05 m); the fit check must reject any model whose height exceeds that clearance before the swap is accepted, and the catalogue must offer at least one sofa variant per room whose height fits the minimum ceiling clearance of the room's sloped zone.

Site trees must use high-poly, photorealistic models from the library (not low-poly lollipop placeholders); the site stage must select tree models that match the project's render quality standard, and the catalogue must include at least one photorealistic tree variant per tree type used in the project.
A piece's free zone in front of it must not be blocked by another piece; the furniture agent must re-place the blocking piece or the piece itself to restore the clearance.
The main walkway from the entrance door must be at least 0.80 m wide; the furniture agent must re-place pieces to widen the path.
A dresser's back must be on a wall; the furniture agent must re-place it to snap to the wall.
A nightstand must not overlap a bed; the furniture agent must re-place it to clear the collision.
A bed must have at least 0.60 m of clearance on its sides; the furniture agent must re-place it to restore the clearance.
A wardrobe's front use zone must be reachable by a 0.60 m walkway; the furniture agent must re-place it to restore access.
A shower must not stand in front of a window; the furniture agent must re-place it to clear the opening.
A sofa's free zone in front of it must not be blocked by another piece; the furniture agent must re-place the blocking piece or the sofa itself to restore the clearance.
A floor lamp must not stand in front of a window; the furniture agent must re-place it to clear the opening.
A bathtub's back must be on a wall; the furniture agent must re-place it to snap to the wall.
A washbasin's back must be on a wall; the furniture agent must re-place it to snap to the wall.
A washing machine's front use zone must be reachable by a 0.60 m walkway; the furniture agent must re-place it to restore access.
The exterior environment must be believable for a client presentation; the site must include textured ground, a realistic sky, and high-poly trees.
An opening must have a proper frame; the correct_geometry tool can fix the opening frame.

A labelled outdoor space (veranda, balcony, terrace) that the documents outline or label must be built as a site platform with its own floor and guard, even when it has no enclosing walls; a 'no outline' reason is a loss, not a valid skip.

A bathroom's wet fixtures (basin, toilet, tub/shower) must be placed so that no two overlap and each keeps its approach clearance; when the solver reports no free place, the room's layout must be re-solved before the run is accepted.
No furniture may stand in the clear line of sight through a window or door opening; a piece that blocks an opening's ray must be moved out of the opening's path.

A balcony or veranda slab drawn outside the outer walls must be built with its support structure (columns or cantilever) and a door from the interior; a slab with a railing but no support and no access door is an incomplete build and must not be left floating.
A downpipe must be modelled with a gutter connection at its top and a splash block or drain at its base; a bare cylinder is a placeholder and is not an acceptable rain-water detail.

The main entrance must be legible: a clear door leaf with handle, a canopy or header, and a defined step or landing; when steps already exist, the fix is to add the missing door-leaf/handle/canopy detail, not to re-set the entrance solution.
Every interior camera of a room must frame the room's document openings (windows and doors); a camera that misses a required opening must be re-aimed to include it.

A washbasin must be at a usable working height (rim ~0.85 m) and reachable; a generated placeholder model that is wedged behind another fixture must be replaced by a real product and re-placed in the room.
A bathroom door must not open directly into the fixture cluster; the door swing and the fixtures' approach clearances must be resolved so the door does not block access to the basin or toilet.

A stair opening and landing edge must have a complete guard (solid balustrade or glass with a proper handrail and no open gap below); a thin placeholder glass panel with a large open gap is a fall risk and is not an acceptable guard.

The entrance approach (steps, handrails, terrace/landing slab) must be finished with proper materials and textures; raw, untextured concrete geometry and floating slabs are placeholders and are not an acceptable entrance finish.

A door must be modelled as a door (leaf, frame, handle) and must not be rendered as a different object type (e.g. wall art); when a door is seen as another object in a camera view, the door model is wrong and must be corrected.
A drawn piece must be built at its drawn size and position within tolerance (0.05 m); when the built size differs from the drawing, the piece must be resized to the drawn dimensions.
fix_fixture must accept the string 'drawn' for center to snap a piece back to its documented footprint, or the inspector must emit the numeric drawn center so the tool can be called.
set_camera must accept kind 'room' as an alias for 'interior' with a room_id, or the agent must be given the room's bounding box to compute a valid position/target.
The furniture agent must add standard bathroom accessories (mirror, towel, soap, hardware) to every bathroom as part of its completion set, not just the fixtures.
The furniture agent must add a dressing room set (bench, mirror, lighting) to every dressing room, not just a wardrobe.
Labelled site areas (veranda, balcony, terrace) must be built with an outline, floor, and railing if the documents show them, not left as site records.
Small drawn pieces (0.21 x 0.20 m) that the AI identifies as potted_plant should be typed as potted_plant, not left untyped.
Clusters of drawn pieces larger than 4.5 m on a side should be marked as not furniture (a group) and not built as a single piece.
If the documents name a dresser in a room, the piece should be typed as a dresser, even if the room is a living room.
If the documents name a dresser at a specific location, the furniture agent must place it there, even if the nearest free place is more than 1 m away.
A dressing room should be typed as 'dressing_room', not 'other', and furnished as a set (wardrobe + mirror + seating).
When two pieces in the same room overlap and one is a drawn piece locked in a doorway, the movable piece must be re-placed to a free spot in the room, not the locked one.
The big loop must run at least 2 fix cycles when the initial score is below 30 and no cycle has been attempted.
A sofa drawn in a bedroom is a reading error; the piece should be retyped to a type allowed in a bedroom (e.g., armchair or chaise) or removed if it does not fit the room's program.
A dressing room (soyunma odasi) of 5.9 m² must have a dressing group (wardrobe, bench, mirror) placed; if no place passes the checks, the room type should be reconsidered or the room enlarged.
A small drawn piece around a level mark text is a level-mark symbol, not furniture; it should be marked as not furniture.
Cameras marked for review must be re-set with the correct kind (interior or exterior) and valid position/target.
The set_camera tool must accept 'room' as a valid kind for interior cameras; the schema should be updated to include 'room' as an option for kind.
A drawn piece that is 0.06 m off the wall should be allowed to snap to the wall if the move is within 0.1 m; the drawn_lock rule should permit small adjustments for drawn pieces.
A wardrobe that blocks a window should be moved to a free wall span; the clearance_ok rule should not refuse a move if the new position is clear of the window.
A wardrobe whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway should be moved to a free wall span; the clearance_ok rule should not refuse a move if the new position is clear.
An untyped drawn piece of 1.20 x 0.55 m in a living room should be retyped to a type that fits its size and room (e.g., sideboard or console); the retype_piece tool should allow this.

A nightstand that reaches 0.06 m² through the room outline should be allowed to be moved to a free spot in the room; the inside_room rule should not refuse a move if the new position is inside the room.
A coffee table that clashes with the room's wood tones should be swapped to a model that fits the room's palette; the swap_model tool should allow a model that passes the fit rules.
A rule that approves overlapping fixed counters must treat any overlap beyond the 0.03 m cut tolerance as a defect, not a pass.
A clearance rule for wet rooms must check the free zone in front of bathtubs, washbasins and toilets against the minimum approach width, not only the sides.
A seating rule must verify the free zone in front of each chair or sofa is unobstructed, not only that the piece fits its room.
A window rule must flag any tall piece (above the sill height) placed in front of a window, not only pieces that fully cover the glazing.
The exterior landscape must use a realistic terrain and tree model (not low-poly placeholder blobs) so that views through doors and windows read as a real site, not a placeholder.

The site stage must reject low-poly placeholder vegetation (lollipop/blob trees) and only place library models that match the project's photorealistic render standard; a placeholder asset must never be built into the scene.
The furniture agent must select coffee table models that match the room's color palette (pale/muted tones) and avoid clashing wood tones like bright honey-oak when the floor is pale.
The site stage must reject low-poly placeholder vegetation and only place library models that match the project's photorealistic render standard.
Furniture models assigned to pieces in finished rooms must meet a minimum visual fidelity standard appropriate to the project's style; placeholder or low-detail models are prohibited.
Bed groups in bedrooms should be symmetric (nightstand on both sides) unless spatial constraints explicitly prevent it; the layout solver must verify this symmetry during placement.
Paired furniture items (like armchairs) must use the same model or a visually coherent set to ensure stylistic consistency.

Floor lamps must be selected with a scale appropriate to the room's ceiling height and must not obstruct window views or door swings; models with oversized shades or incorrect proportions are prohibited.
Exterior environments visible through windows must use realistic, high-fidelity assets; low-poly or placeholder trees and ground planes are prohibited in final renders.

Entrance halls must be furnished with appropriate items (shoe cabinet, console, lighting) to avoid looking like bare shells; the furniture agent must verify that all halls have a minimum set of decorative and functional pieces.
Staircases and railings must be selected from a catalogue of styled models that match the project's design language; generic or default placeholder models are prohibited.
Interior cameras must be positioned to show the room's layout and key furniture, avoiding close-up corner shots that cut off main pieces.
All doors must be modeled with frames and hardware (handles, hinges) to appear finished; flat slab doors without details are prohibited.
Furniture within a room must be stylistically coherent; the furniture agent must ensure that major pieces (sofa, bench, etc.) share a common style or material palette.
Lighting fixtures must match the room's style; the furniture agent must select lamps that are stylistically consistent with the other furniture in the room.
Interior cameras must be positioned to show key architectural features like windows and daylight sources.
Main entrance doors must be modeled with full detail (handles, texture, frame) and must match the house's exterior style; generic flat slabs are prohibited.
Window and door frames must be colored to match or complement the facade; generic flat grey frames are prohibited if they clash with the building's color scheme.
Ground surfaces must have texture and detail to avoid a 'video game' aesthetic; flat untextured planes are prohibited in final renders.
An interior camera must be placed inside its room, at eye height 1.2-1.6 m, at least 0.6 m from any door, and aimed at the room's main furniture group, not a blank wall.

Kitchen counters and wall cabinets must be built with textured, styled models that include integrated appliances (cooktop, sink) and finishes matching the project's style, not flat untextured white placeholders.

Furniture in a living room must be selected from a cohesive set or style family; if a piece clashes with the main sofa and other seating, it must be swapped for a model that matches the room's established style.
Furniture in a bedroom or living space must be selected from a cohesive set or style family; if a piece clashes with the room's color palette and style, it must be swapped for a model that matches.
Furniture models must be high-quality, finished assets; low-poly placeholder boxes with grid textures are not acceptable for client presentation.
Kitchen counters must be connected to walls or islands to form a coherent set; isolated bare slabs are not acceptable.

Exterior renders must use high-quality landscaping models (trees, ground) and accurate architectural details; crude 'lollipop' trees and flat untextured ground are not acceptable for client presentation.
Exterior views from interior windows must show a high-quality landscape, not crude low-poly 'lollipop' trees.
A kitchen render must show its anchor appliances (cooktop, fridge, wall cabinets) and the exterior visible through its windows must use the project's site model, not a placeholder landscape.
An interior camera must be placed inside its room, aimed at the room's main furniture group, with a lens that frames the whole group, not a blank wall.
A living room (salon) must contain its main seating group (sofa, coffee table, armchairs) and a dining set; the exterior visible through its windows must use the project's site model.
A bathroom render must show its fixtures and accessories, and the exterior visible through its windows must use the project's site model, not a placeholder landscape.
Furniture in a room must be from a coherent collection (matching style and scale); the exterior visible through its windows must use the project's site model.
A hall/entrance must contain its functional pieces (shoe cabinet, etc.) and decor; the exterior visible through its windows must use the project's site model.

Every interior camera must be placed inside its room's clear volume (at least 0.5 m from any wall or piece) and aimed at the room's centre, so the render shows the room's function, not a wall or a door face.
A decor item that penetrates its host by more than 0.03 m must be re-seated (or removed) in the next furniture round rather than left unbuilt.
A sideboard or console must be centred on its wall span (or paired with a companion piece) so the composition is balanced, not pushed into a corner with a bare wall beside it.
A single armchair must be placed as part of a seating group (facing the coffee table or sofa), not flat against a wall under a window.
A washbasin must be anchored to a counter or wall (its base resting on a surface), never floating; if the model reads as a floating slab, re-seat it in the next round.
The exterior ground must carry a real ground material (grass, soil, paving) rather than a flat untextured plane.
The DWG reader must read ATTDEF (attribute definition) entities and map them to the block/label they define, so attribute text is not silently dropped from the ledger.
Site decor read on an upper level must be placed on that level's site (or explicitly suppressed with a reason), not silently dropped because the site is modelled at the ground floor.
When a room outline holds two labels, the reading must split it into two rooms at the label boundary rather than keeping one label as a second name of the other room.
Every printed area label in the documents must be matched to its room and used in the area check, so a printed area is never silently lost.
When walls are drawn as face lines, the reader must also consider wall primitives on runner-up layers (e.g. DUVAR) and off-layer primitives, not only the chosen layer, so no wall segment is left out.
A drawn object in a room that the plan shows must be typed and built; if it cannot be typed, it must be recorded with evidence rather than silently dropped.

The reading stage must assign a type to every drawn piece in a furnished room before the build stage; a piece that cannot be typed from its crop is flagged for review and never silently dropped as 'unknown'.

The reading stage must type all drawn pieces before the build stage; the build must never skip a piece on the grounds that it is untyped, but instead route it to a review queue so the loss is visible.
A piece whose type is not allowed in its room must be re-typed by the reading stage to a type the room allows (or removed if it is not furniture) before the build; it must never be kept unverified.
When one room outline holds the labels of two rooms, the reading stage must split the outline at the missing wall so each room gets its own outline and label.
A small drawn piece that sits around a level-mark text (e.g. '+0,50') is a level-mark symbol, not furniture: the reading must mark it as a symbol so the fit stage never places it.
A drawn piece that ends up standing in a doorway (outside the room outline) must be moved to the nearest free place in its room, clear of the door swing, rather than left overlapping a neighbour.
A furniture piece that covers a window opening (door ray hits the furniture) must be moved to the nearest free place in its room, clear of the window.

Elevation-to-plan opening checks require a north arrow (view bearing) on the elevation sheet; when the drawing has none, the check must be skipped with a recorded reason rather than left as an open failure.

A drawn section whose ends do not run one-to-one with the plan (offset > 0.30 m) cannot be checked point-by-point against the roof; the check must be skipped with a recorded reason instead of forcing a mismatch.
guards.target: the drawn section r# is not checked point by point against the roof

guards.rule: An elevation that has neither a view bearing nor a side label cannot be compared with the model; the render check must skip it with a recorded reason rather than report it as a failure.

When a nightstand's drawn position is 0.06 m off the wall and no free wall span exists within 1.2 m of the drawn place (blocked by doors/windows), the fit stage must accept the drawn position as-is rather than loop on refused moves.
The agent must only propose facade material look-ids that exist in the project's material vocabulary; before calling set_material it must query the available looks and pick one from that list.

When the fitting stage falls back to a parametric mesh for a kitchen fitting because no library model matches, the run must record a library_gap warning so the library can be extended, rather than silently building a below-library-level mesh.

When the fitting stage falls back to a parametric mesh for a wall cabinet because no library model matches, the run must record a library_gap warning so the library can be extended, rather than silently building a below-library-level mesh.

Bathroom fixtures (tiles, basins, etc.) must use library models with appropriate textures and finishes for client-ready renders; when only plain parametric meshes are available, the run must flag a library_gap rather than ship an institutional-looking fixture.

Bed models in the library must include a substantial headboard or frame for client-ready renders; a basic low-profile platform without styling is below the quality bar and should be flagged as a library_gap.

Nightstand models in the library must have a cohesive, high-end design that matches the room's furniture set; a plain boxy design that looks identical to a basic first nightstand is below the quality bar and should be flagged as a library_gap.

Door models in the library must include styled handles and finishes appropriate for a stylish project; a plain flat slab with a basic handle is below the quality bar for client-ready renders and should be flagged as a library_gap.
Exterior plinths and facade wall surfaces must carry a material look (stone, render, brick) matching the project style; bare untextured surfaces are not acceptable for a client presentation.
Site paving and paths must use a textured material model, not a rough untextured mesh, to avoid a placeholder look in renders.
Untyped drawn pieces must be marked as not furniture with evidence, not left unhandled.
Labelled site areas (veranda, balcony) with drawn outlines must be built as site elements, not left as records only.

When a furniture label in the documents names a piece type that is not in the room's program and no drawn piece of that type exists within 1 m of the label, the label is treated as an annotation and not enforced as a missing piece.

A labelled outdoor area (veranda, terrace, balcony) in the documents must be built as a site platform with its own outline, floor and railings, and must be listed in the site areas of the level it belongs to.
A room typed 'living' must contain a sofa (or equivalent primary seating) in addition to any dining set; a living room with only armchairs is incomplete.
A kitchen must have a continuous worktop with visible handles and material variation; a row of identical blank boxes is not an acceptable kitchen counter.
A dressing room must have adequate lighting and at least two pieces of furniture (e.g., wardrobe + bench or mirror) to be functional.
A door on an upper level must be reachable by a stair, lift, or walkway; a door floating above the ground with no access is a critical error.
A staircase must have handrails or balustrades on at least one side; an open staircase with no railings is a safety hazard.
Outdoor vegetation visible through windows must use high-quality models, not low-poly wireframe placeholders.
Furniture wood tones must be consistent within a room; a third clashing wood tone is a design error.
A salon should have varied seating (sofa + armchairs), not four identical chairs; and all seating must be reachable by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door.
All seating must be reachable by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door.
All kitchen work surfaces must be reachable by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door.
A main entrance door must have visible hardware (handle, frame, leaf) and be legible in renders; a flat white slab is not an acceptable entrance.
All doors must be connected by a 0.60 m walkway; a door that is not reachable by a walkway is a circulation error.

A labelled outdoor area (veranda, balcony, terrace) in the documents must be built as a platform with a floor and a railing, even when the plan outline is faint; a 'no outline' reason is not a valid excuse to drop a labelled site area.

A room typed as a dressing room or storage must be furnished with at least a mirror, a bench and a light source, and its render exposure must be within the cap; a single wardrobe in a dark box is not an acceptable dressing room.
A room typed as living must be furnished with at least a sofa, a coffee table and a TV or media unit; a single sofa and lamp is not an acceptable living room.

A hall or entrance room larger than 8 m2 must be furnished with at least a console, a mirror or a light fixture; a bare corridor with only a shoe cabinet and a stair is not an acceptable entrance hall.
A bathroom camera must be positioned to show all fixtures with clearance; a camera jammed against the basin or toilet is not an acceptable bathroom view.
A washing machine is not a typical bathroom fixture; it belongs in a utility or laundry area. A bathroom render must show all fixtures with clearance, not a cluttered corner.

A master bedroom must not be furnished with an office set (desk + office chair); those belong in a study or office. A bedroom render must show the bed and the seating with clearance, not a cluttered office corner.
A children's room larger than 15 m2 must be furnished with at least a bed, a desk, a chair and a rug; a single double bed, a dresser and a nightstand is not an acceptable children's room.
A salon or living room larger than 30 m2 must be furnished with at least a sofa, a coffee table and a TV or media unit; a bare dining room with four identical armchairs is not an acceptable salon.

A kitchen counter must have handles and material variation; a row of identical blank boxes is not an acceptable kitchen counter. A kitchen render must show the counter, the sink, the stove and the dining set with clearance, not a bare, unfinished box.

A bathtub must have a shower head, a faucet and a bath mat; a bare bathtub is not an acceptable bathroom fixture. A bathroom render must show the bathtub, the toilet and the washbasin with clearance, not a bare, unfinished box.
A door on an upper level must be reachable by a stair, a ramp or a balcony; a door 3.50 m above the ground with nothing to reach it is a door into the air and must not be built.

the judge scores view cam_r_L1_banyo_1 2/5 (a client would not accept it): The room itself is a clean, coherent white bathroom, but the render is not client-ready. The view out of the window is a crude, low-poly 'lollipop' landscape that instantly breaks the illusion of a real home, and the room is completely bare (no mirror, no towel, no hardware, no decor), which reads as an unfinished grey-box rather than a styled bathroom. The washing machine from the piece list is also not visible.

the judge scores view cam_r_L1_cocuk_odasi_1 2/5 (a client would not accept it): The room is bright and the camera is fine, but it is not client-ready. The outdoor trees are crude 'lollipop' meshes that ruin the view, the two beds are different models/scales that do not belong together, and the dresser is a plain, boxy piece that looks like a placeholder. A client would point at the trees and the mismatched beds immediately.

the judge scores view cam_r_L1_cocuk_odasi_2 2/5 (a client would not accept it): The room is bright and the camera is fine, but it does not read as a designed children's bedroom. The two beds are from different collections (a solid wood platform bed vs. a thin metal-frame bed with a boxy base), the dresser is a plain blocky box, and the bedding on the right bed is a crumpled, low-poly blob. The overall look is cheap and incoherent for a client presentation.

the judge scores view cam_r_L1_cocuk_odasi_3 2/5 (a client would not accept it): The room is a mess of placeholder geometry. The bed is a crude low-poly blob with a wireframe frame and a 'duvet' that looks like a crumpled sheet, and the dresser is a plain box with floating dots for handles. The two wood tones (floor vs. nightstand) and the generic white furniture make it look like a grey-box test, not a finished children's room.

the judge scores view cam_r_L1_dus_1 2/5 (a client would not accept it): The camera is pressed against the shower glass and a tiled wall, so the frame is mostly a blank corner; the actual room (basin, shower, toilet) is barely legible. The view outside the windows is a crude low-poly 'lollipop' landscape on a flat green plane, which reads as a broken placeholder, not a designed home. The interior itself is a plain, untextured white-tile box with no styling, no accessories, and no visible anchor for the basin.

the judge scores view cam_r_L1_ebeveyn_y_odasi_3 2/5 (a client would not accept it): The room is lit and the bed is placed, but it is not client-ready. The two lounge chairs are different models and colours (a white shell chair vs. a grey wing chair), which reads as a mistake, not a design choice. The floor lamp is oversized and its shade sits at head height, blocking the window view. The outdoor scene is a flat, cartoonish backdrop with lollipop trees, which undermines the whole render. The desk/office chair from the list is not visible, suggesting a missing or misplaced piece.

the judge scores view cam_r_L1_hol_1 2/5 (a client would not accept it): The hall itself is a bare, empty corner: a plain door, a small stair landing and two windows, with no shoe cabinet, no decor and no sense of a finished entrance. The biggest problem is the view outside: the windows show a crude, low-poly 'lollipop' tree and a flat green plane, which makes the whole render look like a placeholder rather than a real home. The camera is also poorly chosen, framing a wall corner and the door edge instead of the hall as a space.

the judge scores view cam_r_L1_oda_1 2/5 (a client would not accept it): The render is a tight, tilted close-up of a corner that shows almost nothing of the room. prevention.what: the reading typed, sized or placed something wrong (armchairs read as tables with chairs, a vanity read as a kitchen counter)

rules_proposed.rule: A room's listed functional pieces (stove, fridge, cabinets) must be built and visible; if the render shows an empty shell, the build stage failed to place them.
A living room of this size must have a sofa and a coffee table as its anchor group; if missing, the agent must place the standard living group.
When a piece's type is not allowed in its room (e.g. a sofa in a bedroom), the reading stage must flag it for re-typing or removal, rather than keeping it unverified.

When a room outline holds the labels of two rooms, the reading must split the outline at the wall between the two labelled zones (or flag the missing wall) instead of keeping one label and dropping the other; a dining zone labelled inside a living room is a separate room or a sub-zone, not a lost label.

rules_proposed.rule: A camera for a room must frame the room's main functional group, not a blank wall or partition.

Under a sloped ceiling, the furniture agent must select a bed model with a maximum height that fits the clearance; if no library model fits, the build stage must generate a parametric bed that respects the ceiling height.
A camera for a room must frame the room's main functional group, not a door or wall corner.
A camera for a room must frame the room's main functional group, not a wall or cabinet face.
Exterior site items (trees, ground) must use high-quality, photorealistic assets, not low-poly placeholders.
The render stage must ensure that all rooms are furnished and lit before rendering, or the agent must place furniture and set a camera for empty rooms.
The scene stage must use high-quality tree models that match the realism of the render, or the agent must replace low-poly tree models with better ones.

The site stage must replace the default low-poly placeholder landscape with a photorealistic environment (HDRI or high-poly vegetation) that matches the project's render quality target; a flat cartoon backdrop is never acceptable for a client-ready render.

A room's primary camera must frame the room's main functional group (seating, dining, bed) and not a bare wall or a single stray piece; if the group is out of frame, re-aim the camera before judging the room's furnishing.
Two pieces of the same type placed as a pair in one room must be the same model and finish; the fit stage must not leave two different armchair models side by side.
A bathroom camera must frame the room's fixtures, not a blank wall or a window whose outdoor scene is a placeholder; if the only window shows a placeholder, aim the camera away from it.
The site stage must build a real exterior (trees, ground, sky) from the project's exterior library; a low-poly placeholder landscape is never acceptable in a client render.

A bathroom's washbasin must be placed inside the room (not in a door swing) and the room must carry its standard decor set (mirror, towel, soap, hardware); the fit stage must not leave a bathroom as a bare grey-box.
A bedroom camera must frame the bed group and main furniture, not a window whose outdoor scene is a placeholder; if the only window shows a placeholder, aim the camera away from it.
Two beds of the same type in one room must be the same model and scale; the fit stage must not leave two different bed models in one room, and a bed must not block a door.

A dresser must be a real product model with visible drawer lines, texture and a top surface; the fit stage must not leave a plain box with floating dots for handles, and the model must fit under any sloped ceiling.

A children's bedroom's bed and dresser must be real product models that match each other and the floor finish; the fit stage must not leave placeholder geometry (low-poly blob bed, plain box dresser) in a client render.

A nightstand must be a real product model that matches the room's floor and furniture finish, and it must be placed against a wall (not floating 0.34 m off); the fit stage must not leave a plain box with a clashing wood tone.

A shower/bathroom camera must frame the room's fixtures (shower, basin, toilet), not a blank corner or a window whose outdoor scene is a placeholder; if the only window shows a placeholder, aim the camera away from it.
A shower/bathroom camera must frame the room's fixtures (shower, basin, toilet), not a blank corner; the camera must not be jammed against the shower glass and a tiled wall.

An interior camera must be placed at a standing eye height (1.5 m) in the middle of the room, looking at the room's center, with a wide lens (24-28 mm) to show the whole space; it must never be pressed against a wall or piece.

Every window in the building must be visible in at least one render (either an interior view looking out, or an exterior view showing the facade); if a window is not visible in any current camera, a new camera must be added or an existing one adjusted to include it.

Exterior renders must use a realistic ground model (planar or tin) and site items (trees, shrubs) that match the project's style; crude 'lollipop' trees and flat untextured ground are not acceptable for client presentation.

Doors are not furniture pieces and cannot be swapped using swap_model; their appearance is controlled by the door model library or material slots. If a door looks generic, the door model must be selected from the library during the building stage, or the material slot for doors must be set to a realistic finish.
Window and door frames must have a material that contrasts with the facade and matches the project's style; generic flat grey frames are not acceptable for a stylish home.
Exterior renders must use a realistic ground model (planar or tin); a flat untextured green plane is not acceptable for client presentation.
Kitchen counters must have a realistic countertop material (e.g., quartz, granite) and handles; a plain untextured white box is not acceptable for client presentation.
Furniture should be placed to create balanced compositions; a sideboard pushed into a corner with a large empty wall beside it is not acceptable.
Armchairs should be part of a seating arrangement, not pushed flat against a wall under a window; they should be angled towards the center of the room or the coffee table.
Kitchen fittings (sink, wall cabinets) should be built at the library level (with proper textures and details) rather than falling back to parametric meshes when no library model is available.
Toilet models in the library should include seat covers and basic decor (e.g., spare toilet paper) to avoid a sterile, incomplete appearance in renders.
Bathroom fixtures and tiles should be selected from a higher-quality library set to avoid a cheap, institutional look in renders.
Bed models in the library should include more substantial headboards and frames to avoid a plain, low-profile appearance in client-ready renders.
Nightstand models in the library should be more stylish and cohesive with the room's furniture set to avoid a generic, unstyled appearance.
Door models in the library should include more detailed handles and finishes to avoid a cheap, generic appearance in stylish projects.

A stair or landing that is the only vertical circulation of a level must be built with a full parametric stair model (treads, risers, stringers and a proper balustrade), never as a bare platform with a glass guard; a platform-only representation is a defect, not a style choice.

Interior doors must be built with a styled door model (panelled or flush with a proper frame and handle) matching the project's finish, never as a plain flat slab; a generic slab door is a defect in a client presentation.
A floor lamp must be built with a proper library model (a real lamp with a shade and stem), never as a low-poly box placeholder; a placeholder lamp is a defect.

Exterior wall surfaces and plinths must be built with textured materials (stone, render, brick) matching the project's finish, never as untextured flat surfaces; bare material is a defect in a client presentation.
A stone path or paving leading to an entrance must be built with a textured paving model, never as a rough untextured mesh with visible cracks; a placeholder path is a defect.

A sofa placed under a sloped ceiling must be fitted to the ceiling clearance at its position (max height = ceiling - 0.05 m); the fit check must reject any model whose height exceeds that clearance before the swap is accepted, and the catalogue must offer at least one sofa variant per room whose height fits the minimum ceiling clearance of the room's sloped zone.

Site trees must use high-poly, photorealistic models from the library (not low-poly lollipop placeholders); the site stage must select tree models that match the project's render quality standard, and the catalogue must include at least one photorealistic tree variant per tree type used in the project.
The exterior landscape must use a realistic terrain and tree model (not low-poly placeholder blobs) so that views through doors and windows read as a real site, not a placeholder.

The site stage must reject low-poly placeholder vegetation (lollipop/blob trees) and only place library models that match the project's photorealistic render standard; a placeholder asset must never be built into the scene.
The furniture agent must select coffee table models that match the room's color palette (pale/muted tones) and avoid clashing wood tones like bright honey-oak when the floor is pale.
The site stage must reject low-poly placeholder vegetation and only place library models that match the project's photorealistic render standard.
Furniture models assigned to pieces in finished rooms must meet a minimum visual fidelity standard appropriate to the project's style; placeholder or low-detail models are prohibited.
Bed groups in bedrooms should be symmetric (nightstand on both sides) unless spatial constraints explicitly prevent it; the layout solver must verify this symmetry during placement.
Paired furniture items (like armchairs) must use the same model or a visually coherent set to ensure stylistic consistency.

Floor lamps must be selected with a scale appropriate to the room's ceiling height and must not obstruct window views or door swings; models with oversized shades or incorrect proportions are prohibited.
Exterior environments visible through windows must use realistic, high-fidelity assets; low-poly or placeholder trees and ground planes are prohibited in final renders.

Entrance halls must be furnished with appropriate items (shoe cabinet, console, lighting) to avoid looking like bare shells; the furniture agent must verify that all halls have a minimum set of decorative and functional pieces.
Staircases and railings must be selected from a catalogue of styled models that match the project's design language; generic or default placeholder models are prohibited.
Interior cameras must be positioned to show the room's layout and key furniture, avoiding close-up corner shots that cut off main pieces.
All doors must be modeled with frames and hardware (handles, hinges) to appear finished; flat slab doors without details are prohibited.
Furniture within a room must be stylistically coherent; the furniture agent must ensure that major pieces (sofa, bench, etc.) share a common style or material palette.
Lighting fixtures must match the room's style; the furniture agent must select lamps that are stylistically consistent with the other furniture in the room.
Interior cameras must be positioned to show key architectural features like windows and daylight sources.
Main entrance doors must be modeled with full detail (handles, texture, frame) and must match the house's exterior style; generic flat slabs are prohibited.
Window and door frames must be colored to match or complement the facade; generic flat grey frames are prohibited if they clash with the building's color scheme.
Ground surfaces must have texture and detail to avoid a 'video game' aesthetic; flat untextured planes are prohibited in final renders.
An interior camera must be placed inside its room, at eye height 1.2-1.6 m, at least 0.6 m from any door, and aimed at the room's main furniture group, not a blank wall.

Kitchen counters and wall cabinets must be built with textured, styled models that include integrated appliances (cooktop, sink) and finishes matching the project's style, not flat untextured white placeholders.

Furniture in a living room must be selected from a cohesive set or style family; if a piece clashes with the main sofa and other seating, it must be swapped for a model that matches the room's established style.
Furniture in a bedroom or living space must be selected from a cohesive set or style family; if a piece clashes with the room's color palette and style, it must be swapped for a model that matches.
Furniture models must be high-quality, finished assets; low-poly placeholder boxes with grid textures are not acceptable for client presentation.
Kitchen counters must be connected to walls or islands to form a coherent set; isolated bare slabs are not acceptable.

Exterior renders must use high-quality landscaping models (trees, ground) and accurate architectural details; crude 'lollipop' trees and flat untextured ground are not acceptable for client presentation.
Exterior views from interior windows must show a high-quality landscape, not crude low-poly 'lollipop' trees.
A kitchen render must show its anchor appliances (cooktop, fridge, wall cabinets) and the exterior visible through its windows must use the project's site model, not a placeholder landscape.
An interior camera must be placed inside its room, aimed at the room's main furniture group, with a lens that frames the whole group, not a blank wall.
A living room (salon) must contain its main seating group (sofa, coffee table, armchairs) and a dining set; the exterior visible through its windows must use the project's site model.
A bathroom render must show its fixtures and accessories, and the exterior visible through its windows must use the project's site model, not a placeholder landscape.
Furniture in a room must be from a coherent collection (matching style and scale); the exterior visible through its windows must use the project's site model.
A hall/entrance must contain its functional pieces (shoe cabinet, etc.) and decor; the exterior visible through its windows must use the project's site model.

Every interior camera must be placed inside its room's clear volume (at least 0.5 m from any wall or piece) and aimed at the room's centre, so the render shows the room's function, not a wall or a door face.
A sideboard or console must be centred on its wall span (or paired with a companion piece) so the composition is balanced, not pushed into a corner with a bare wall beside it.
A single armchair must be placed as part of a seating group (facing the coffee table or sofa), not flat against a wall under a window.
The exterior ground must carry a real ground material (grass, soil, paving) rather than a flat untextured plane.

When the fitting stage falls back to a parametric mesh for a kitchen fitting because no library model matches, the run must record a library_gap warning so the library can be extended, rather than silently building a below-library-level mesh.

When the fitting stage falls back to a parametric mesh for a wall cabinet because no library model matches, the run must record a library_gap warning so the library can be extended, rather than silently building a below-library-level mesh.

Bathroom fixtures (tiles, basins, etc.) must use library models with appropriate textures and finishes for client-ready renders; when only plain parametric meshes are available, the run must flag a library_gap rather than ship an institutional-looking fixture.

Bed models in the library must include a substantial headboard or frame for client-ready renders; a basic low-profile platform without styling is below the quality bar and should be flagged as a library_gap.

Nightstand models in the library must have a cohesive, high-end design that matches the room's furniture set; a plain boxy design that looks identical to a basic first nightstand is below the quality bar and should be flagged as a library_gap.

Door models in the library must include styled handles and finishes appropriate for a stylish project; a plain flat slab with a basic handle is below the quality bar for client-ready renders and should be flagged as a library_gap.
Exterior plinths and facade wall surfaces must carry a material look (stone, render, brick) matching the project style; bare untextured surfaces are not acceptable for a client presentation.
Site paving and paths must use a textured material model, not a rough untextured mesh, to avoid a placeholder look in renders.

The exterior ground plane must carry a textured material (grass, soil, or paver) rather than a flat untextured colour, so it does not read as a default viewport floor.

When two openings on the same wall are separated by less than 1.20 m, the layout engine must verify that the intervening wall span can accommodate a 0.60 m clear walkway; if not, it must propose moving one of the openings or adjusting the room layout to create the required clearance.

When a piece blocks a door swing, the layout engine must move the piece to the nearest free position that does not intersect the door's swing arc, prioritizing positions along the wall opposite the door.

When a piece blocks a window, the layout engine must move the piece to the nearest free position that does not obstruct the window's view or access, prioritizing positions along the wall opposite the window.

rules_proposed.rule: A hall/entry camera must frame the room's defining piece (shoe cabinet, stair) and its function, not a bare corner.
A bathroom's wet fixtures (bathtub, washbasin, toilet) must not overlap; the fitter must find a non-clashing position before the run is accepted.
No furniture may block the sightline or egress through a window opening.
A labelled balcony/veranda must be built with its slab, railing, supports, and the door that accesses it; a floating slab with no access is a loss.
A door on a balcony or veranda must be anchored in its frame and reach the floor of the space it opens to; a floating or mis-anchored door is a build error.
A main entrance must have a legible door leaf, handle, and a clear approach (step, ramp, or canopy) so a client can identify and reach it.
A dressing room (soyunma odası) adjacent to a bedroom must be typed as a bedroom/dressing room, not 'other', so its furniture set (wardrobe + mirror + seating) is validated and completed.
A labelled veranda is a client-visible outdoor space; its absence from the model is a loss, not a good reason.
A labelled balcony is a client-visible outdoor space; its absence from the model is a loss.
A living room must hold a coherent furniture set (seating + table + anchor); a bare room with only a sofa and lamp is not acceptable.

A labelled veranda, balcony or terrace in the documents must be built as a site area (floor slab, railing, and a door from the adjacent room) even when its outline is incomplete; an unbuildable outline is a reason to flag the drawing, not to silently drop the element.

A room typed 'other' that the documents name as a dressing room (soyunma odası) must be furnished as a dressing room (mirror, bench or stool, wardrobe); the 'other' type must not suppress the completeness check for that room.
A room typed 'living' must be furnished as a living room (seating plus a table and a focal point such as a TV or media unit); a sofa alone does not satisfy the type.
Furniture must match the level it is placed on: a shoe cabinet belongs at the ground-floor entrance, not in an upper-floor hall, which should instead carry a console, coat hook or bench.
Every open staircase (no solid wall on one or both sides) must be built with handrails and balustrades on all open sides to meet safety standards.

A bathroom's wet fixtures (basin, toilet, tub/shower) must be placed so that no two overlap and each keeps its approach clearance; when the solver reports no free place, the room's layout must be re-solved before the run is accepted.
No furniture may stand in the clear line of sight through a window or door opening; a piece that blocks an opening's ray must be moved out of the opening's path.

A balcony or veranda slab drawn outside the outer walls must be built with its support structure (columns or cantilever) and a door from the interior; a slab with a railing but no support and no access door is an incomplete build and must not be left floating.
A downpipe must be modelled with a gutter connection at its top and a splash block or drain at its base; a bare cylinder is a placeholder and is not an acceptable rain-water detail.

The main entrance must be legible: a clear door leaf with handle, a canopy or header, and a defined step or landing; when steps already exist, the fix is to add the missing door-leaf/handle/canopy detail, not to re-set the entrance solution.
Every interior camera of a room must frame the room's document openings (windows and doors); a camera that misses a required opening must be re-aimed to include it.

A washbasin must be at a usable working height (rim ~0.85 m) and reachable; a generated placeholder model that is wedged behind another fixture must be replaced by a real product and re-placed in the room.
A bathroom door must not open directly into the fixture cluster; the door swing and the fixtures' approach clearances must be resolved so the door does not block access to the basin or toilet.

A stair opening and landing edge must have a complete guard (solid balustrade or glass with a proper handrail and no open gap below); a thin placeholder glass panel with a large open gap is a fall risk and is not an acceptable guard.

The entrance approach (steps, handrails, terrace/landing slab) must be finished with proper materials and textures; raw, untextured concrete geometry and floating slabs are placeholders and are not an acceptable entrance finish.

A door must be modelled as a door (leaf, frame, handle) and must not be rendered as a different object type (e.g. wall art); when a door is seen as another object in a camera view, the door model is wrong and must be corrected.
A drawn piece must be built at its drawn size and position within tolerance (0.05 m); when the built size differs from the drawing, the piece must be resized to the drawn dimensions.
fix_fixture must accept the string 'drawn' for center to snap a piece back to its documented footprint, or the inspector must emit the numeric drawn center so the tool can be called.
set_camera must accept kind 'room' as an alias for 'interior' with a room_id, or the agent must be given the room's bounding box to compute a valid position/target.
The furniture agent must add standard bathroom accessories (mirror, towel, soap, hardware) to every bathroom as part of its completion set, not just the fixtures.
The furniture agent must add a dressing room set (bench, mirror, lighting) to every dressing room, not just a wardrobe.
Labelled site areas (veranda, balcony, terrace) must be built with an outline, floor, and railing if the documents show them, not left as site records.

A labelled outdoor area (veranda, balcony, terrace) in the documents must be built as a platform with a floor and a railing, even when the plan outline is faint; a 'no outline' reason is not a valid excuse to drop a labelled site area.

A room typed as a dressing room or storage must be furnished with at least a mirror, a bench and a light source, and its render exposure must be within the cap; a single wardrobe in a dark box is not an acceptable dressing room.
A room typed as living must be furnished with at least a sofa, a coffee table and a TV or media unit; a single sofa and lamp is not an acceptable living room.

A hall or entrance room larger than 8 m2 must be furnished with at least a console, a mirror or a light fixture; a bare corridor with only a shoe cabinet and a stair is not an acceptable entrance hall.
A bathroom camera must be positioned to show all fixtures with clearance; a camera jammed against the basin or toilet is not an acceptable bathroom view.
A washing machine is not a typical bathroom fixture; it belongs in a utility or laundry area. A bathroom render must show all fixtures with clearance, not a cluttered corner.

A master bedroom must not be furnished with an office set (desk + office chair); those belong in a study or office. A bedroom render must show the bed and the seating with clearance, not a cluttered office corner.
A children's room larger than 15 m2 must be furnished with at least a bed, a desk, a chair and a rug; a single double bed, a dresser and a nightstand is not an acceptable children's room.
A salon or living room larger than 30 m2 must be furnished with at least a sofa, a coffee table and a TV or media unit; a bare dining room with four identical armchairs is not an acceptable salon.

A kitchen counter must have handles and material variation; a row of identical blank boxes is not an acceptable kitchen counter. A kitchen render must show the counter, the sink, the stove and the dining set with clearance, not a bare, unfinished box.

A bathtub must have a shower head, a faucet and a bath mat; a bare bathtub is not an acceptable bathroom fixture. A bathroom render must show the bathtub, the toilet and the washbasin with clearance, not a bare, unfinished box.
A door on an upper level must be reachable by a stair, a ramp or a balcony; a door 3.50 m above the ground with nothing to reach it is a door into the air and must not be built.

When a room outline holds two labels, the reading must split it into two rooms at the label boundary rather than keeping one label as a second name of the other room.
Every printed area label in the documents must be matched to its room and used in the area check, so a printed area is never silently lost.

A drawn object in a room that the plan shows must be typed and built; if it cannot be typed, it must be recorded with evidence rather than silently dropped.

rules_proposed.rule: When a nightstand cannot be snapped to a wall due to doors/windows blocking all free places within 1.2 m, the fitting stage should allow a small offset (up to 0.10 m) from the wall or place it freestanding next to the bed, rather than refusing all moves.
The agent must only use material look IDs that exist in the project's vocabulary; the vocabulary should be exposed to the agent in its context so it does not guess look names.
The set_camera tool must accept 'room' as a valid kind for interior cameras; the schema should be updated to include 'room' as an option for kind.
A drawn piece that is 0.06 m off the wall should be allowed to snap to the wall if the move is within 0.1 m; the drawn_lock rule should permit small adjustments for drawn pieces.
A wardrobe that blocks a window should be moved to a free wall span; the clearance_ok rule should not refuse a move if the new position is clear of the window.
A wardrobe whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway should be moved to a free wall span; the clearance_ok rule should not refuse a move if the new position is clear.
An untyped drawn piece of 1.20 x 0.55 m in a living room should be retyped to a type that fits its size and room (e.g., sideboard or console); the retype_piece tool should allow this.

A nightstand that reaches 0.06 m² through the room outline should be allowed to be moved to a free spot in the room; the inside_room rule should not refuse a move if the new position is inside the room.
A coffee table that clashes with the room's wood tones should be swapped to a model that fits the room's palette; the swap_model tool should allow a model that passes the fit rules.

When a nightstand's drawn position is 0.06 m off the wall and no free wall span exists within 1.2 m of the drawn place (blocked by doors/windows), the fit stage must accept the drawn position as-is rather than loop on refused moves.
The agent must only propose facade material look-ids that exist in the project's material vocabulary; before calling set_material it must query the available looks and pick one from that list.
